title: Devanagari
hook: the week it gets worse: two letters crash into one knot
tomorrow: can you read a holy text on your own?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devanagari's vowel signs: the e on top, the u below, the long a at the side, every letter dressed in its vowel. Today, letters that stop standing alone.

Halfway through learning anything, a guitar, a new job, a driving test, there's often a stretch where it gets worse before it gets better. Devanagari has that stretch, and it has a shape. Two consonants meet with no vowel between them, and instead of standing side by side, they crash into one knot of ink. A reader who just got comfortable stares at a letter that isn't on any chart.
screen: `IT GETS WORSE BEFORE BETTER.` → `TWO CONSONANTS, NO VOWEL.` → `ONE KNOT OF INK.`

segments.voice: The knot is called a conjunct, and it isn't a new letter. It's two you already know, holding on. The first has lost its a, the way a virama would take it, so it leans into the next. Look at karma, the first word of the Gita's line. Between ka and ma there's an r with no vowel. So the r doesn't stand on the line at all. It climbs up and sits on top of the ma as a little hook, like a curl of hair. Karma: ka, then ma wearing the r. Other knots squeeze one letter's half into the next, or stack them. The move is always the same: find the two inside, say them together. And when a stretch of learning gets hard, the Gita has a word for what to do. Arjuna tells Krishna the mind is restless, stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna doesn't argue. He says it can be held by abhyasa, practice, and by letting go. Not talent. Coming back, again, a little at a time. That's exactly what a conjunct asks. The first time, it's a knot. After enough mornings, it's two letters holding on.
screen: `A CONJUNCT: TWO LETTERS HOLDING ON.` · `KARMA: THE R CLIMBS ON TOP.` · `FIND THE TWO INSIDE.` · `ABHYASA: COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you're learning that's in its harder stretch. Name, silently, what you want from it; then the knot that's in the way; then one small time and place you'll come back to it. Let each of the three sit for a few slow breaths before the next.
Devanagari: a script whose consonants join into conjuncts when no vowel comes between them.
Hold on to it: Devanagari, where a knot of ink is just two letters holding on to each other. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Learners usually meet conjuncts after the basic letters and vowel signs, and practice them in common words like karma and dharma, where the r rides on top of the next letter.

chat.meaning: A conjunct is two consonants joined because no vowel comes between; in karma the r rides on top. Krishna's word for the rest: abhyasa.

karma.meaning: action; the first word of the Gita's line

abhyasa.meaning: practice: coming back again and again

Arjuna.meaning: the warrior Krishna teaches in the Gita

Krishna.meaning: the teacher in the Gita, worshipped by Hindus as God

notes: Answers 1432's question. Gita 6.34 (Arjuna: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind) and 6.35 (Krishna: by abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, dispassion, it is held) are paraphrased; 'letting go' stands for vairagya. Confirm.

Reph (the r riding above the next consonant) named only in the trapdoor. 'Karma' as the first word of 2.47: the text has karmaṇi (in action), written in sandhi as karmaṇy-; the lesson calls it karma for simplicity. A scholar may prefer 'karmani'. The sandhi itself is taught on day 1437.
Life shape: the friend's fork ('three weeks into piano') is a new situation, not a factual claim.
